jobLines.text: List 3 flights from San Francisco to Los Angeles

goal:
Do the job below from the input files, then write one JSON file per numbered line.

The input files (label: file):
  - flights: input/flights.txt

For each numbered job line N, write ONE file output/steps/N.json: a JSON object with exactly these keys.
  "text"  — your answer for that line, as a string.
  "cites" — an object: for each input you drew on, its label as the key and a list of {"claim", "quote"} as the value.
            "claim" is one thing your text relies on; "quote" is words copied EXACTLY from that input (spacing and
            ** or __ marks do not matter). Every number in a claim must also appear in its quote.
  In each claim, copy every number, time and price exactly as the input writes it (for example "9:27 AM", not "09:27"),
  because the check matches the numbers in your claim against your quote.
A job line the brief below marks as a FACTS line is different: its file holds ONLY {"results": [{"quote": "...", "values":
{"<fact>": "<value>"}}]} — one result per thing found, one quote copied exactly from the text of that one result, the values written as the quote
writes them; no "text" and no "cites". A line the brief marks as a TEXT line keeps "text" (free words), and every number in it
must be copied from a quote of an earlier facts line.
Write nothing outside output/, and never edit the files under input/. The file must be complete, valid JSON: a file cut
off before its closing brace counts as not written.

The job, line by line:
1. List 3 flights from San Francisco to Los Angeles
   rule: under $450; not a red-eye; nonstop

Job line 1 is a FACTS line. Write output/steps/1.json as {"results": [{"quote": "...", "values": {...}}]} and nothing else — no "text", no "cites".
  One result per thing you find in the input "flights": exactly 3 results.
  "quote": ONE quote per result, copied exactly from that result's own text in the input (at most 4000 characters) — never joined from two results.
  "values": one entry per fact below, written exactly as the quote writes it (for example "9:27 AM", not "09:27"; "389", not "389.00").
    - from price — an amount in US dollars, right after "From", must be under 450 US dollars
    - cheapest price — an amount in US dollars, right after "Cheapest from", must be under 450 US dollars
    - departure time — a time, right after "Departure time:", must be between 5:00 AM and 9:00 PM
    - origin — no value to write; the quote you copy must say "Leaves San Francisco International Airport"
    - destination — no value to write; the quote you copy must say "arrives at Los Angeles International Airport"
    - departing date — a date, right after "departing", must be between 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-12

The plan the person confirmed: Confirm line 1 (output/steps/1.json) lists exactly 3 flights, that each listed flight's price is under $450, that each listed flight's departure time is between 5:00 AM and 9:00 PM (the AI's proposal), that each leaves San Francisco International Airport and arrives at Los Angeles International Airport on 2026-11-12 as quoted from the input, and that the input's \"Cheapest from\" price is under $450.

notes: The person's ~ rule "not a red-eye" cannot be verified from the input: the input holds no "red-eye" word. The only thing I could check is the departure time the input does hold (after the input's label "Departure time:"), as a between 5:00 AM and 9:00 PM range. That number is MY proposal, not the person's, and it is marked aiProposal on the fact.
The person's ~ rule "nonstop" cannot be verified: the input holds no "nonstop" phrase for this search.

The person's ~ rule "under $450" is carried on both money facts (from-price and cheapest-price), quoted from the input using the input's own label words "From" and "Cheapest from" and the input's own unit "US dollars", not the person's words.

The rule "not a red-eye" was written by the person as one thing; the confirmed plan splits the price side of that rule across check #2 (each flight's price) and check #7 (the "Cheapest from" price), so both money facts carry ~ rule 1.

The input's own words were used instead of the person's: the person wrote "San Francisco" and "Los Angeles", the input writes "Leaves San Francisco International Airport" and "arrives at Los Angeles International Airport" — those exact phrases are the origin and destination facts.

The departing date fact uses the input's label "departing" (the input writes "2026-11-12"), not the person's wording. I gave it a between 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-12 range marked as the AI's proposal, because the input states one date per flight and the fact shape "date" takes a rule only as a limit.
The look could not find any label for a "nonstop" phrase in the input, so nothing is checked for it.
